author: charles
sigSummary: On a Sunday in Alexandria, expecting a cavalry raid, Charles watches Black men impressed off the street to throw up breastworks across every road to the wharves, where government stores wait — while his own regiment digs a defensive trench around the city. Word arrives that Alexander has come safely out of the fight, and Charles turns to an ordinary errand: sending $11.20 in greenbacks to buy his brother a watch. Burdick is back, promoted to Captain.
transcription:
May 19, 1863
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

I was very much gratified yesterday to receive a letter from Alexander. Have been anxiously expecting a letter from either you or him for some time. He has probably written you that he came safely out of that fight and is back in his old camp. In his letter he makes me to write to you for the money to buy a watch. I will buy him a watch and either take it to him or send it by express. Wish you would send me $11.20 of Alex's money by mail; greenbacks if you can get them, for a watch for him. I hope Alex did not keep you in suspense as long as he kept me about his safety. Don't know why he did not write to me sooner.

Our Lieut. has just made a new law for our Co. It is this: Men absent from roll call to be drilled by the corporal on duty next day. The man, or son,

[page break]

can, for I need it very, very, very much. Give my regards to all the boys from Champlain.

Your aff. Brother,

Alexander F. Hubbell

P.S. We are camping in the same place as when you were here.

Albert Cook was here while I was gone to Aquia C. Am sorry that I did not see him. Burdick is back and is promoted to Captain. Another Capt. is now Lt. Col. and Capt. Strain is Major and the Major is Col.

We expect a cavalry raid in this city. Today is Sunday and all the n****rs in the street were impressed this forenoon and set to work throwing up a breastwork across each street leading to the wharves. A vast amount of government stores are in buildings along the wharves and the rebels would like to destroy them. Our reg't. has been for some time at work digging a trench around the city. This trench answers two purposes. It will be hard for the cavalry to cross it and our infantry will find

author: charles
sigSummary: Charles crossed three lines of guards on the Alexandria wharf to reach Aquia Creek and surprise his brother Alexander with a $15 silver lever watch. Alexander, color bearer in the recent fight, told Charles he felt bad he could not stand with his regiment, having been detailed to guard a baggage train; Charles told him he was lucky. Back in Alexandria, contrabands were impressed on a Sunday to throw up stockades of green hardwood logs, eight to ten feet high, against an expected cavalry raid.
transcription:
May 31, 1863
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

I received your letter two or three days since containing eleven dollars. Since I last wrote you, I have been to Aquia Creek to see Alex. Found him well and much surprised to see me. The watch that I surprised him he was delighted with. It was a double cased silver lever watch and I paid $15. for it. Bought it of a Serg. in our Co. who said $20. for it, but as he was hard up, sold it for $15. cash down. I only had $11 and he waited for the other $4 till I rec'd, the money you sent. So I owe him and his watch one week before I received the money from you. Staid over night with him. They are fixed up quite comfortable. Should not be surprised if they staid there some time as I don't think Hooker will make an advance very soon. Alex is in the same old of his camps, Fort or Net large as ever. He was color bearer in the fight. He is detached from the reg't. and is Serg. in the ambulance Corps. Alex told me he was not in the fight, but was detailed to guard a baggage train. Said he felt bad that he could not be in the fight with his reg't. I told him he was lucky. The men said they laid flat on their bellies, the shells whistling over them and they hugged the ground close. They were lying behind a breastwork that was thrown up with him classes and bayonets. I had some trouble getting on board the boat to come back. There were three lines of guards on the wharf. I fell in behind our guard that was going on the boat and passed two lines of guards, but the third stopped me, thinking I was not a guard as I had no gun. Our Serg. told him I belonged to his, but they told me I could not pass. After waiting nearly two hours on the wharf the guards let all go through in a rush without showing their papers and the Captain redirected the passes at the gangway of the boat. I had no pass, but our Serg. told the captain how it was and he let me on. Then I was stopped on the wharf, I was afraid I would have to wait till the next day, but I did not. Alex told me that you had applied to his Lieut. Col. for his discharge. But neither of us thought it would do any good. I told him if his discharge was offered him he had better accept it, but he did not say that he would.

Albert Cook was here while I was gone to Aquia C. Am sorry that I did not see him. Burdick is back and is promoted to Captain. Another Capt. is now Lt. Col. and Capt. Strain is Major and the Major is Col.

We expect a cavalry raid in this city. Today is Sunday and all the n****rs in the street were impressed this forenoon and set to work throwing up a breastwork across each street leading to the wharves. A vast amount of government stores are in buildings along the wharves and the rebels would like to destroy them. Our reg't. has been for some time at work digging a trench around the city. This trench answers

[page break]

it a good breastwork. We have cannon placed at different points on the inside of the ditch. A few days ago a nine months reg't. came here. Their time is out next month. They have been at work digging this ditch also and a lot of n****rs were impressed to work also. These negroes are contrabands. I said that at each street breastworks are being thrown up, but they are not breastworks, but stockades which are logs of wood placed end on end close to each other. A train of cars is now here loaded with green hardwood logs. The men are going to work all night at the stockades. This is Sunday night work, but then whiskey is plenty for the laborers and the rebels may make a raid any time. There will be some very heavy gates on these stockades. They are to be 8 or 10 feet high. A part of it is done now and every little way a log is left shorter than the others for the soldiers to fire through. The streets are stockaded about two blocks from the river.

An incomplete letter from Charley

..... 30 .....

author: alexander
sigSummary: Lt. Col. Redington sang through the shellfire at Chancellorsville, Alexander tells his mother and sister — using "the screams of the shells as they passed over his head as a key to pitch his voice on," just as he had at Antietam. The slight, erect colonel is "a man of courage." Writing from camp near Aquia Creek Landing, Alexander signs off "in haste": June 4th orders have come to march with three day's rations, "probably merely a reconnoissance."
transcription:
June 3rd, 1863
Camp near Aquia Creek Landing

Dear Mother and Sister:

I received your welcome letter of May (something) today, and am much pleased that you have at length heard from me. Tell me when you next write whether it was my first or second letter you received. I am glad you have heard from Lt. Col. Redington, and sorry for your disappointment. He is a very fine man, and I like him much.

So, Miss Fannie, you are quite curious to know how Colonel Redington found out your name. I can explain it in no other way than that when looking over the mails he has seen your address on different letters I have written you. It is also quite likely that Capt. Ransom in his conferences with the colonel relative to me thought it necessary to mention your name. You ask me to describe Colonel Redington. He is about the minimum height, rather slender and very erect. He is quite a man of business — a great bargainer, which will go to make us a hero, you know. But what is most of all, he is a man of courage. In the last battle at Chancellor he was singing away at a great rate, using the screams of the shells as they passed over his head as a key to pitch his voice on. He did the same at Antietam as they were passing over a hill a key to pitch his voice on.

So the young gents at Champlain are displaying their patriotism by burning boxes and powder (their mothers are very imprudent; powder is a dangerous thing), and ringing bells. How generous of them to do so much for their beloved country — still it is asking almost too much of them. "The evening is damp and the smell of powder very pernicious to the health — it would have a tendency to give them the ague."

June 4th — We have orders to march with three day's rations. We leave our camp as it is. It is probably merely a reconnoissance. Luther's father is here.

Yours in haste,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Will you now and then send me a stamp?

author: charles
sigSummary: Charles writes from Alexandria of a magazine at Fort Lyons that exploded the day before, killing twenty and wounding as many a mile or two from his regiment's camp, a great noise still in his ears as he reports good health and easy swims in the Potomac. Then the harder business: "I think that you ought to apply at once for Henry's back pay and bounty." He was killed, without a doubt — file before the others do, or the family waits.
transcription:
June 10, 1863
Alexandria

Dear Mother:

I received your welcome letter of June 2nd yesterday and was glad to hear from you. Enclosed is a few lines that I received from Alex. Received two more letters from him dated the 7th this morning. He wrote me the first letter that I received today because he wanted to buy a gold ring for a man, and he wrote the second because he forgot to put the measure of the ring in the first, and as he forgot to put it in the second and was on duty he requested Amos Luther to write to me and enclose the measure, which he has done, so that I read three letters or notes from Alex and Amos this morning. Amos says his father has been there to visit him and stayed two days. He went to Falmouth. Amos' letter was dated June 8th and says they expect to move soon.

One of the magazines attached to Fort Lyons exploded yesterday killing twenty and wounding about the same number. It made a great noise. This fort is a mile or two from this city and is in sight of our reg't. camp. But I guess I have told you this before. I have had some good swims in the Potomac. My health is good and I hope that you and Frances are enjoying good health.

When I visited Alex I staid over night with him; staid about one day. He was well. I think it would be pleasant for you and Frances to make a visit together to Charlotte while M. Smith is there. Can't Frances get some one to take her two classes while she is gone and put on her French till she gets back? It would be a pleasant visit for you both. How do Charlotte affairs come on? Have not heard anything about them for a long time.

I think that you ought to apply at once for Henry's back pay and bounty. For if those who apply first receive the money you will have to wait a good while. He was killed, without a doubt.

We have an hours drill every morning before breakfast and drill a while after supper, also I have plenty of reading here, more than I can read. I see the daily papers quite often. Welky in our tent, has got the History of Rome, also of France, also of United States. Small volumes, each of them. I have not read them, but intend to do so.

I must close as I am in haste.

Your Aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

author: charles
sigSummary: Mother has left home for Charlotte, and Charles writes from Alexandria to ask the question that haunts the whole letter: "How do you get along alone and where are you staying?" He has had only two papers and one very short note since she left, and supposes she is still away — then the page ends mid-sentence. Dated June 29, 1863, two days before Gettysburg, this fragment catches a scattered family reaching across silence.
transcription:
June 29, 1863
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Frances:

I have received two papers from you since Mother left home. How do you get along alone and where are you staying? Received a very short letter from Mother a few days since which I answered. Suppose she is still at Charlotte, but

[TEXT CUTS OFF — end of PDF]

author: alexander
sigSummary: On Independence Day from a field near Gettysburg, Alexander Hubbell tells his mother that God has preserved his life through another terrific battle and he has not received a scratch — though his regiment lost fifty-two, eleven killed and forty-some wounded, in fighting that ran from 2 P.M. on the 2nd until midnight. He reports a great victory, then adds the day's grim work: "We are burying our and the rebel's dead today."
transcription:
July 4th, 1863
Near Gettysburg, Penna

Dear Mother:

God has again in his great kindness preserved my life through another most terrific battle. I have not received a scratch. The reg't. lost fifty-two — eleven killed and forty-some wounded. We commenced fighting about 2 P.M. on the 2nd inst. (We had been under artillery fire for some hours previous) and continued fighting until about midnight. We fought nearly all day yesterday. If God spares my life, I will endeavor to write you again soon and give you particulars.

Please tell Capt. Ransome that Milebus Ayres of my Co. was killed and Sergeant Brookway and Private John Tickle were wounded. We have gained a great victory. We are burying our and the rebel's dead today. Love to all.

Your aff. Son,

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. Our Captain deserves especial praise for his bravery.

author: charles
sigSummary: On the Fourth of July the whole garrison at Alexandria paraded under the Brig. Gen'l. and his staff — sweat streaming, whiskey rations before and after, a speech almost no one could hear. Charles writes home unaware: "I should like to hear from Alex. Have not heard from him for a long time." A deserter from his own company sits in jail, betrayed when his wife's reply revealed his hiding place in St. Lawrence County.
transcription:
July 6, 1863
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

I read a letter from you a few days since and was glad to learn that you were enjoying yourself. Am glad that Grandmother recommended you hope for I run one you are at home by, this time. Think her visit will be pleasant for you.

There was a grand parade of all the troops in this place on the fourth of July. Our Brig. Gen'l. and staff rode at the head of the column. The soldiers did not find it much fun to march around the streets all the forenoon with the sweet streaming off from us. But the men did not grumble much because they had some whiskey given them before we started and after we got back. We marched with our reg'ts. There was a band of music and a short speech was made from the platform side of the street, but very few heard it.

I should like to hear from Alex. Have not heard from his for a long time. He must have had a hard time in his march to Penna. Perhaps the want of writing materials is the reason he doesn't write. A deserter from our Co. on furlough was caught and brought back here and is now in jail. I don't know what will be done with him. He was living in St. Lawrence County and wrote to his wife at Plattsburgh. She answered the letter, and as they now knew where he was, the deserter was nabbed. He has a brother in our Co.

I send you James' letter with mine. He deserves credit for his application. I answered his letter this morning. Am glad that you are attending to Henry's bounty and back pay. Suppose you apply late you will have to wait some time for it. Have you seen anything of Brend Miner and A. Cook? How do the Savage family get along? Tell Frances to give my regards to David Savage. Blackberries are now very thick here. In our company alone is near the Potomac, some of our men have obtained a pass from our Lieut. and borrowed a boat and then crossed the river to Maryland after blackberries and cherries. The pass has to be shown at the gunboat in the river. I have not been yet as I have been on duty when they went, but I intend to go over the river berrying soon.

What do you think of the war now since our great victory over Lee? I have not seen today's paper, but I will get one. Hope Alex is all right.

Is the pony getting fat and what do you think he will bring when sold? How does our deer of a cow get along? Does she trouble Sid? If she does I could poke her as she does not tear down a fence but merely jumps it. A poke will stop that.

You had better sell my old clothes if you have not done so, or the moths will eat them up. A good many in our Co. have sent clothing home by express. Mr. Steais wrote to ask to send a box if he could. A soldier when he has too much of a load will sell cheap or give away his overcoat of blanket and our men get them and send them home. Have you paid that church tax? It ought to be paid. Take some of my money and pay it. What do you think of Mrs Cynthia Bourns's husband? Jim Lucas heard that the Savages said he had only one fault and that was he was not a Christian.

Does Silas get any business? I don't believe he will emigrate to Chicago. There is Mrs. Brink passing the summer. I think I have asked a good many questions, but you must ask if you would know. Today it rained nearly all the forenoon very hard. How does Frances go to Charlotte? I received the two papers that she sent. Wish she would write. Must close as I am in haste.

Your aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

author: alexander
sigSummary: Two stands of colors taken at Gettysburg, and seven rebel officers stretched out in a row before the company — Alexander writes his mother from near Crampton's Gap, having come through the battle "unscratched." The old 60th "beat the rebels gloriously," yet he braces for more: "We will doubtless fight tomorrow or next day. My life is in God's hands." Only miles from the Antietam ground, he hopes to find his brother Henry's grave.
transcription:
July 8th, 1863
Near Crampton's Gap, Md.

Dear Mother:

I wrote you immediately after the battle of Gettysburg (through which I came unscratched) but am somewhat afraid you may never get the letter and accordingly I now write you again to let you know of my welfare.

We beat the rebels gloriously in that battle. The old 60th took two stands of colors from the enemy. We stretched seven rebel officers out in a row in front of the company. We will doubtless fight tomorrow or next day. My life is in God's hands. His will be done.

We are only seven or eight miles from the Antietam battle ground. If possible, I shall visit it and endeavor to find out something about Henry. Love to all.

Your Aff. Son,

Alexander F. Hubbell

author: charles
sigSummary: Writing from Alexandria a week after the New York draft riots, Charles asks his mother dryly, "Don't you think New York has been a pleasant place to live in the last few days?" The draft has delighted the soldiers — their one objection being the law letting drafted men buy their way out, since "$300 doesn't grow on every bush." Between worry over James after Hooker's forced march and a review in the hot sun, he recounts crossing the river for half a bushel of blackberries.
transcription:
July 20th, 1863
Alexandria, Va.

Dear Mother:

I have not received a letter since July 8th and I am a little vexed at your long silence. But I try to excuse you by thinking that you and Frances are both busy. I have not written because I have been waiting to hear from you. Have not heard from James for some time. Have you heard from him? I have not heard a word about him since the army left Aquia Creek. He must have been nearly worn out after Hooker's forced march.

Capt. Rich left yesterday for Champlain. I heard that he is going to get the band of the 26th N.Y. Reg't. for Gen. Slough; also that he is going to try to get the drafted men from Champlain and vicinity to come into the three Plattsburgh companies in our reg't.

Steais and Douglas have had a list from home of the big bugs drafted in Champlain and Alex D. heard that there were some long faces there. Sid and Silas are lucky to escape, for $300 doesn't grow on every bush. There was a Plattsburgh paper here with a printed list of the drafted men in our county. Nothing has pleased the soldiers so for a long time as the draft. The only objection is the law that the soldiers have that men can get off by paying for it.

Tomorrow there is to be a general review of all the troops in Alexandria. We don't like it much as we marched in the hot sun on the 4th of July enough to satisfy us. Our woolen clothes are not cool, you know. We expect to be paid today. Our company is having a good time and we don't expect to leave here very soon. We would not have much a good time if we were with the reg'ts. Nine o'clock Sunday morning we have inspection. We get up at five and are all the morning getting ready. Each man unslips knapsack and comes it to show his kit. It takes a great deal of rubbing and brushing to get ready for inspection.

How is your and Frances health? Hope it is good, also hope that you both are prospering finely. My health is good. How is Grandmother McNeill? and all the rest in Charlotte? Is Frances gone visiting? Guess she has, as she doesn't write, but then she would have more leisure on a visit than she has at home. What is the news from Champlain? Have you heard from James lately? If you have will you send me his letters and I will return it. I saw a day or two since that there are now twenty vacancies in West Point owing to that number not passing the examination.

Don't you think New York has been a pleasant place to live in the last few days? I mob rules as well. I guess a good many citizens skedaddled from the city. I think a good many that are drafted in Champlain will pay $300 before they will come out as soldiers. Has Frances put out any of my money at Savages since the first time I sat fall? How much did she get out then? Have you done anything further about Henry's money? Well, that claim agent did you go to?

We have had a good deal of rain here lately but now the water is hot. I never saw such a place for blackberries as it is here. Have been over the river to M., one after berries. Eight or ten of us got a pass and borrowed a boat and then after showing our pass at the gunboat in the river we were soon across. Staid an hour or two and came back with over half a bushel of berries. They are very thick towards the convalescent camp two or three miles from here.

Hope that you and Frances will both write soon. Hoping that you both are trying to enjoy yourselves and don't worry about us boys. I will close by saying that I remain

Your Aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

author: charles
sigSummary: Charles writes from comfortable barracks on Capitol Hill, his company detached from the regiment for six months after a sudden night move out of Alexandria — and confesses he only learned "Alex came safely out of that Gettysburg fight" from Mother's letter, never from Alexander himself. The mail had failed at the moment it mattered most. Meanwhile an orderly sergeant, a corporal, and the cook sit under arrest for stealing and selling ten days' rations the night before the march.
transcription:
July 25, 1863
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I received your welcome letter of July 16th. Was glad to hear from you and Frances. Rec'd a letter from James dated the 18th. He writes in good spirits. Am glad that Alex came safely out of that Gettysburg fight. Until I rec'd your letter did not know anything about him. Have not heard from him yet, but I will write him soon.

I suppose you have heard from Mr. Steais that we have left Alexandria. It was a sudden and unexpected move. The first we knew of it, about 6 o'clock one night some of our men said they saw our reg't marching towards Wash. with knapsacks. A little while after a Co. came to relieve us and gave us an order to report to Wash. Our 1st Lieut. want to see the Major that commanded our Co. We were ordered to leave that night. But we did not leave until next morning. A good many thought that we would leave immediately for the front. We did not, though, but are now in comfortable barracks. The Reg't. came here on foot which is about 8 miles, but our Co. came on a steamboat. The day before we left ten days rations were drawn for the company as — did not expect to leave. During the night somebody stole nearly all the rations and sold them. They thought we were going to leave we could draw some more rations somewhere else. Yesterday an orderly sergt. with another sergt. and corporal James Lucas and the cook were arrested and are to be tried for selling our rations. Four of our Co. under arrest. If found guilty they will be severely punished. Jim Lucas told some one that he was there when the rations were stolen.

We were detached from the Reg't. six months. Some say that we will stay here some time if we behave ourselves. Our Col. told some of the men that if they did not want to carry a knapsack this summer they must behave themselves. The Col. is very strict about everything. A private in our Co. has been tried by courts martial and sentenced to lose one month's pay and do one day's hard work for always being dirty. We are now in the Capitol of the U.S. and can't do as we have a mind to. No officer or soldier can leave the camp ground without a pass.

How much was the pea tax that you paid? Frances did right in putting out that money. We are receiving our pay today. Enclosed is a twenty dollar check. I want you to use as much of my money as you want. Will you tell me who has rented the farm this year and how much he pays? I have forgotten, but suppose it is Murray. Am much obliged to Frances for her letter. They are few and far between, but then she has a good excuse as she is so busy. Hope she will keep her promise and write me a long letter. I need not tell you to write often because you generally do, although not lately. The weather is dry and hot.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell

author: alexander
sigSummary: At Camp near Warrenton Junction, Alexander Hubbell saves his fiercest news for the postscript: he fired "fifty or sixty shots into the very teeth of the rebels at Gettysburg," who charged "with hoots and yells" but "stopped their clack pretty quick." With the regiment down to about two hundred men, he cheers the draft, scorns those who got exempt — "Shame on their cowardly, craven hearts" — and asks his mother quietly for a little U.S. money.
transcription:
Camp near Warrenton Junction
July 30, 1863

Dear Mother:

I have at length found leisure and materials to write you a few lines. We are now having a few days of rest after our long and painful marching and much we need it. I was nearly worn out when we reached this place, but am now fast gaining strength. Oh, of what we have endured you can have but a faint conception; nevertheless it has been done cheerfully and much more will be done to put down this war. The whole army is wonderfully pleased at this draft taking place and much merriment is excited as some familiar name is observed in the list of the drafted. Several commissioned officers and six sergeants have gone from this regiment after drafted conscripts. Each Co. is recruited up to eighty men, I believe. We have only about two hundred men left. I presume we shall be on the move soon, though we may wait for the conscripts.

Please acknowledge to Mrs. Boyle the receipt of those papers and thank her warmly for me. You can have no idea what a blessing they are to myself and comrades. Your Tribunes and Mrs. Boyles' papers are now going the rounds of the Co. much to their pleasure and benefit. Mrs. Boyle sent me a paper with the list of drafted. Company H has a jolly time over it.

So Albert Cook and the rest of the 34th are at home, eh! I wish them much joy. Tell Albert that I am again in the same region where I saw him last and that it is the same hot, parched up country as of old. I had hoped I should never see this part of the country again, but Providence has decreed it otherwise. The "Sunny South" is no home for me. It is too confoundedly sunny to suit my taste. I do hope and pray that this war may end soon. I hope Charleston will fall down. It is just what is needed to crush the rebellion, I think. I am sorry to hear that H. D. and others have got exempt and don't see how they have done it. How will their places be supplied? Will another draft take place? Shame on their cowardly, craven hearts. I hope the returned soldiers will give it to them as they deserve.

I will endeavor to write you often if I can procure the materials which it will be very difficult to do as I have no money. Mother — I am sorry to say it — if you can, will you send me a little? If you can, be careful and send no other than U.S. money, as no other is good here. Love to all. I shall direct this letter to you, Miss Fannie.

Yours with much affection

Alex F. Hubbell

P.S. I had the satisfaction of firing about fifty or sixty shots into the very teeth of the rebels at Gettysburg. They charged on us with hoots and yells, but stopped their clack pretty quick. They did screech, but it was out of the other corner of their mouths.

author: alexander
sigSummary: Charles, on guard at the R.R. Depot in wartime Washington, watches the provost's men arrest a boy of about nineteen fleeing the draft in a captain's coat too large for him — stolen or bought, he can't say. His regiment guards two prisons and the depot, James Lucas is reduced to the ranks for stealing rations, and each man is now marched to a hospital window for a daily whiskey ration he thinks is laced with quinine.
transcription:
August 16, 1863
Capitol Hill Barracks
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

It is a long time since I wrote you and the reason is we are all very busy. We are on guard from one to two days at a time. Still I might write while on guard if I could carry the writing materials with me. I have received no letter from you for a long time also, but I suppose I can't say anything as I have not written you.

Our Reg't. guards two prisons and has a guard at the R.R. Depot, also has a camp guard, and besides a large number of men go down to the provost marshals every night and sleep there on the floor to be ready if wanted. The provost marshal's is over a mile from here. We have a good many men go every day to the city hall where the draft has been taken place and they are now examining the drafted men or their substitutes. Most of them get substitutes. Every night the men that the examining board are listed under a strong guard and taken to a barracks that is strongly guarded. A good many citizens are caught at the R.R. Depot trying to run away from the draft. Yesterday they arrested, while I was at the depot, a young fellow I should think about nineteen years old. He was dressed as a captain, only his coat was too large for him. He may have stolen or bought the coat. I have not heard how he came out.

I received a letter from Mary McNeill a few days since. Guess I will answer this letter soon. I waited so long before answering the other that I thought she would not answer it. Have not heard from Alex yet; wish he would write. Have you heard from him lately; if you have I will write to him again. I think James is not getting along so badly as you said in your last letter. I expect a letter from him soon. Did you receive that $20.00 check that I sent you two or three weeks since by mail? You said nothing about it in your last letter. As we can get plenty of reading here you need not send me the Observer; send only the Tribune once in a while.

They are now giving furloughs in this reg't. I think I told you that James Lucas was reduced to the ranks and loses a month's pay for being concerned in stealing rations. A corporal here has an easier time than a private, as he only changes the guard, and does not stand guard. Also he does not come on duty as often as a private. Capt. Burdick has resigned and is going home very soon, I think. Every day a small quantity of whiskey is given to each man that wants it. Some kind of medicine is in it; I think it is quinine. They only commenced giving it out a day or two ago. All in the Co. that want it are marched to the hospital to get it from an open window. Some would drink the whiskey, no matter what was in it, for the sake of the spirits. I write in haste so I must close.

From your Aff. Son,

C. F. Hubbell

P.S. Please write soon.

author: charles
sigSummary: The draft has taken place — and from his Capitol Hill barracks, Charles tells Mother to "break up keeping house" this winter and go to Charlotte, gently proposing the end of the family home. His regiment guards two prisons and the depot while fifty men daily escort drafted conscripts from City Hall. He presses her to settle Savage's debts, and ventures a verdict: "Jeff is about played out, but there will be a good deal of guerilla fighting yet."
transcription:
August 21, 1863
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I was very glad to receive a letter from you and James and Frances yesterday. Have been expecting a letter from you for some time. Am glad that you and Frances are both well. My health is good.

I like living in barracks better than in tents as we have plenty of room and can keep our clothes and guns cleaner, and they are warmer in winter, I guess, and I know they're cooler in summer. There are plenty of windows and now the window sashes are taken out to let in the air. Tents, unless they are raised up to let in the air, are hot as an oven in summer. But there is one objection to our barracks, which is bed bugs. A good many of the men say they can't sleep in the barracks on account of them and they sleep on the ground close to the barracks. But I am lucky to have a bunk where there are none, at least I have not felt any as yet or anyway. If there were bed bugs, I believe I should sleep in the bunk as I don't think it would be healthy for me to sleep on the ground exposed to the heavy dew.

We have plenty of guard duty to do. Our reg't. guards two prisons, the R.R. depot, and does other duty besides. The draft has taken place and every day about fifty of our men go to the City Hall where the drafted men or their substitutes are examined, to keep order and take the men passed by the board to the barracks where they are kept. We on get passes to go into the city when we are not on duty. I have had one pass and have been to the Capitol, also to the patent office. Have not been to church yet as I have been on duty every Sunday but one. The Chaplain talks to those that want to hear every Sunday night. Benches are placed in the yard and the Chaplain, with his hearers around him and caps all off, proceeds to business.

I think it would be a good plan to break up keeping house this winter and you go to Charlotte. You could pay them something for your board. And the woods could be left in care of some good person. Frances would like to leave home, I suppose, and leave Montcalm. It might be more pleasant for you both to break up.

About the cow you sold Mr. Boyle, I would not be small with him as he has been a good friend of ours. I do not know what cows are worth, but I should think $40 a great price for her. I am glad you are going to settle up with Mr. Savage. Last fall Savage rendered their acct. to you; it was $16.55. Joel Savage's separate acct. was then $37.49, but was not rendered to you. Then there will be interest on these debts since last fall. The Surrogate wrote you last summer that there was nine or ten dollars in his office due you. I forget the amount. I guess it was sent to my Flave or some one else. But they never got it. It would be well to get this.

I think it very strange that Sid and wife and the rest of the family can't live in that big house. Do you think Sid will get rich farming? I guess all that Mr. Clark told you some time ago about our good luck that was coming won't come true. Guess if we get any more land in Champlain, it will be by paying for it. What do you think of the war? Do you think it will be a thirty year's war now? I guess Jeff is about played out, but there will be a good deal of guerilla fighting yet.

I am much obliged to you and Frances for your long letters. Hope you both will write often. I will write Alex today. I remain

Your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell

author: alexander
sigSummary: Marching through Maryland, Alexander passed over part of the Antietam battle ground — within half a mile of where he and the 34th had fought. "Oh! how I longed to leave the ranks and hunt for some trace of Henry, but it was impossible." Discipline held him in line, and he buries the loss between a joke about pulling his close-cropped hair and word that Sergt. Howes was reduced to the ranks for drunkenness.
transcription:
August 25, 1863
Ellis Ford

Dear Sister Frances:

I presume you would like to pull my hair right lustily — (rather a difficult matter, by the way, as it is not over an inch or two in length) for not writing you before. I plead guilty and promise all sorts of good things if you will let me off this time. Let me know immediately as I am afraid that my cranium (through fear of the pulling) will soon be in as critical a position as that of a certain ancient philosopher whose head a certain ill omened bird mistaking for a stone dropped an enormous turtle on it. How the old fellow must have hopped, eh! Well, now, Miss Fannie, if you do not wish me to hop as lustily as he did, write immediately. (That's a good way to get a letter!)

All is quiet today along the lines of the Rappahannock, but we expect stirring times before many weeks. Shouldn't wonder if Lee paid us a visit. But a truce to war.

How does Mr. Simonds flourish and that lame wrist of his? Hope it is not so bad but what he can use the rod to castigate the "young ideas" of Champlain. If this should be the case, please recommend for me a very popular mode of punishment we have done here, i.e., hanging a man up by his thumbs and allowing only his toes to touch the ground.

How do Cook and the other returned soldiers flourish? Hope they have good times. My regards please give to all that you know. I believe that I never told you that during the march in Maryland, I passed over a part of the battle ground of Antietam, where we were at one time during the day and about half a mile from where we and the 34th fought. Oh! how I longed to leave the ranks and hunt for some trace of Henry, but it was impossible. Not far from there we halted and loaded and formed our line of battle. Skirmishers were thrown out and we marched a short distance when we halted and commenced throwing up intrenchments, etc., etc.

I believe I also forgot to mention that Sergt. Howes of my Co. has been reduced to the ranks for drunkenness and that Amos Luther has been promoted to his place. This occurred some time since. It slipped my mind when I wrote before. Tell Mother that I sent her fifteen dollars by express a few days since. Wish I could have sent more. Tell her to use it to pay taxes or whatever else she pleases. Love to all.

Your aff. Brother,

Alexander F. Hubbell

author: alexander
sigSummary: Mother's letter wounded him before any rebel could: she feared he had forgotten her. "Could you for a moment suppose I could ever forget my old home and my Mother? Never, never," Alexander writes from Ellis Ford, blaming letters rifled beside the railroad. Across a hundred-yard river, he and the rebel pickets study each other "very composedly," past firing — "some of the Rebs are pretty nice fellows, much to my surprise."
transcription:
Sept. 3rd, 1863
Ellis Ford

Dear Mother:

I received your letter of the 20th of August tonight — and feel — Oh! so bad. I do not blame you for writing as you do, but I should like to know the reason why you do not get my letters. Mother, during the last two months I have received but two letters from home. I have felt so bad that I had but small heart to write. I wrote to you and to Frances and to Albert Cook. Sent a paper to Frances, to Capt. Ransom, to Cook, and to Ingram, and heard nothing from any of you. The letter I received tonight has written on the envelope "60th N.Y. Vol. — not 6th Corps." Direct to the 2nd Division, 12th Army Corps, and then there can be no mistake.

Mother, could you for a moment suppose I could ever forget my old home and my Mother? Never, never. I love my Mother better than life itself. There is nothing I would not endure for your sake, and it makes me feel so badly to think that you could for a moment think I had forgotten you. It is thoughts of you and my old home that have sustained me in our long marches. No, Mother, I can never forget you.

One of the Divisions in this Army has been warned in "general orders" not to send valuable matter in the mail as a number of letters from their Division were found beside the railroad rifled of their contents. Measures were then being taken to ferret out the thief. My letters may have disappeared in a similar manner.

We are now camped near the river in a very pleasant spot, with plenty of nice cool water close at hand. A small stream runs close by in which we wash, etc. The Reg't. is now obliged to go on picket every other day. A rather funny thing happened one night before last. About twelve or one o'clock the picket opposite me fired two shots into his own men surrounding us, wounding one man severely. It was criminal to hear his groans. The river is about one hundred yards wide and very shallow in most places. It is just about the same as the river at G. The rebel picket stands on one side and I on the other. We sit and look at each other very composedly as we have both learned better manners than to fire at each other. The rebels are very anxious to exchange papers with us, but we have strict orders not to do it. If the settling of the war was left to the soldiers we would do it in short order. Some of the Rebs are pretty nice fellows, much to my surprise.

Now, Mother, please write me often. I promise you I will, and I hope they will not be miscarried or destroyed. I was very much worn out when we reached here. The last day we marched thirty-five miles. I have been blessed with any number of Job's comforters, of late. My candle is about burnt out. Love to all and a great deal to Frances. She seems to doubt my love for her. Shall write her soon. Her letter needs attention. I came within an ace of tearing it up before I had read three lines. As I continued reading, my wrath cooled down measurably and when I had finished I felt more like giving her a kiss than boxing her ears. Please write soon. Much love to Albert.

Your aff. son,

Alex F. Hubbell

author: charles
sigSummary: Garrison life at Capitol Hill Barracks: Charles writes Mother that his health is good, troubled only by bed bugs he's fighting with unguentine and hot water. He relays word from James — 65 new cadets to fill the West Point vacancies left by the seceded South. Then a Methodist church beside camp turns vivid: a soldier of his company shows up drunk, the ladies turn up their noses, and one man dubs it "a religious drunk."
transcription:
Sept. 7, 1863
Capitol Hill Barracks
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I received your welcome letter of Aug. 28th in due time. Was very glad to receive so long a letter. I did not know as four weeks had gone by without my writing, but I suppose I was waiting for you to write. You know you were not very prompt in writing at that time. My health is very good. Have nothing to bother me except bed bugs and other animals, but as I am using unguentine and hot water, expect to be rid of them soon.

Have you seen Mr. Burdick yet? I saw him the night he left, but did not feel very well then as I had a headache. Was all right the next morning, though. Mr. Burdick was in very high spirits at the thought of going home for good. When he was home before, he said that he pushed my letter under the door as no one was in. I sent no letter by him this time as I had no time to write. I am sorry that he resigned.

Received a letter from James Sunday with your last letter. In it was his picture which I think looks very well. I think you are mistaken about Mr. B. trying to injure James. He stands on his own merits there. James says there are to be 65 new cadets to fill vacancies caused by the south seceding. Says the plates are used rather rough.

Frances wants to know about that fair correspondent. Well, she is anything but fair. Among a lot of Beardslee's pictures I saw none here, therefore I know. I guess Corporal Beardslee wants the papers that she sent nearly a month old. I suppose that was the reason, but as I did not do it, had only two or three papers from her. He is saving of his money and would like some one to do it to save him the expenses.

Yesterday I attended the Methodist church which is close to our camp. One of our Co. was there last evening and he was a disgrace to the regiment, as he visited his whiskey in the church. The ladies looked blank and turned up their noses. One of our men called it a religious drunk. He had preaching a last evening in the yard. Benches were brought out of the mess rooms so that we sat down in a square. The Chaplain is sick, but a preacher with newspapers of different denominations gave us a good sermon; also the newspapers.

There are a lot of old Harpers Magazines and some books forming a small library which we can draw from every week, so that we have plenty of reading. Our 1st Lieut. has come home on a furlough. Capt. Rich is somewhere near Fonda attending to conscripts, I believe.

author: charles
location: Camp Davis, Capitol Hill, Washington, D.C.
sigSummary: James will get along well enough, his brother Charles guesses from Camp Davis on Capitol Hill, though he doubts the cadet will graduate high. Sickness runs through the regiment; a stout corporal of about twenty-one is suddenly dead, and Pet Steais lies in the hospital with something wrong in his chest. Then the garrison's dark comedy: an illiterate man who mailed his sweetheart his entire $200 in pay and bounty, only to learn she married another and spent it all.
transcription:
Sept. 15, 1863
Camp Davis, Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I received the Tribune two or three days since, and yesterday rec'd. a letter from Alex. He was well and having a pleasant time.

I think you have the wrong idea about the no. of demerits that the cadets can get before they are found. I came across one of James' old letters and in it he said that they can had 150 demerits the first six months, also the same for the second six months of the first year. After that 100 demerits in six months will discharge them. It takes 150 demerits in six months to discharge them the first year. Have you heard from James lately? How is he getting along and how did he dispose of all his photographs? I think James will get along well enough, but don't expect he will graduate very high. Has Hiram I. got his appointment yet?

There is a good deal of sickness in this regiment. A corporal from our Co. died a few days since. He was apparently a stout, rugged fellow, about twenty-one years old, I should think. Alex Douglas is not very well he is this finest, but you will have a chance to see him for yourself, as he expects to go home soon on a furlough. Pet Steais is in the hospital which is close to the barracks. They live well in the hospital and he comes over to the barracks sometimes. Something is the matter with his chest, I believe.

The boys in our Co. laugh a great deal at one of our men, also pity him because he was such a fool as to do as he did. It seems he was engaged to a girl before he enlisted and he has sent her pay, bounty, and other money to the amount of $200. A few days since he heard that she was married and had spent all the money. He is an ignorant fellow and can neither read nor write. The men told him often that she would have served him so and that he had better send it to his father. When asked how his girl is, he replies that she has gone to Hell. This word is rather common here used in this way "keep on if you think there is no hell."

There is a good deal of talk about our leaving this place soon. I don't know whether we will or not. We are to receive our pay today. If we do leave here I shall be sorry, for it is a good place. A short time since we learned that we could draw books from the soldier's free library in the city. Since then we have drawn books.

author: alexander
sigSummary: A brigade execution of two deserters, witnessed up close: one man took three volleys to die, and both sat upon their own coffins beside open graves while every off-duty soldier was marched past to "learn a lesson." Alexander calls them "poor fellows" yet judges the killings "salutary," with five more men shot elsewhere that day. He notes it was the anniversary of Antietam, and braces for battle: "I am in God's hands and the thought gives me comfort."
transcription:
Sept. 18, 1863
Raccoon Ford
Rapidan River, Va.

Dear Mother:

I have just witnessed the execution of two deserters. They belonged to this Brigade. Every man that was not on duty was obliged to be there. One of the poor fellows was obliged to shoot three times before they killed him. They sat upon their coffins beside their graves where they were shot. After the execution we were all marched by the coffins that we might see them and learn a lesson. I think these examples will have a very salutary effect upon the army. Five others were shot today in other parts of the army.

Company H. presented a sword to Captain Delaney today. Did you receive the fifteen dollars I sent you not long since? We are being paid again today. I shall send twenty dollars this time. I received your letter of the 12 inst. last night. It does me good to hear from you. Please write often. Tell Frances I want longer letters from her. I shall write her soon if possible. Yesterday was the anniversary of the battle of Antietam. I presume I shall be in another battle soon. I am in God's hands and the thought gives me comfort — does it not you? I trust that my life will be spared to see this unholy rebellion crushed and the country restored to prosperity and happiness again. What joyful days those will be!

Love to all. I have received James' photograph. It does not look very natural to me. He has changed very much, I think.

Your aff. son,

Alexander Hubbell

P.S. I send the express receipt I received for the fifteen dollars, peradventure you have not received the money.

author: charles
sigSummary: Charles writes from Capitol Hill with a soldier's eye for the small mercy: it is not his turn for the detail guarding prisoners out at 6:30 with three days' rations, "and I am glad of it, for the nights are cold and it might rain." Drill runs twice a day now. He urges Mother to refuse a pension: with three sons in the army, "it looks bad."
transcription:
Sept. 25, 1863
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I read your welcome letter of Sept. 21 yesterday, also one at the same time from Mary McNeill. By the way, I don't exactly fancy corresponding with a cousin I have never seen. She says the three families there are all well. What families are they? Max John, Charles and Wm. McNeill? How near do these families live to each other?

About that pension. I would not apply for one if I were you. With three sons in the army it looks bad if you should draw a pension.

Part of the duty of the regt. has been taken off; since then, which is four or five days since, the regt. has drilled every afternoon and there is Co. drill in the morning from 6 to 7 before breakfast.

Not long since the orderlies' call was beat and me soon learned why. It was made by our orderly detailing 12 men and 2 corporals from our Co. to go off somewhere. Each Co. furnish their proportion of men and they are to start at 6:30 A.M. tomorrow with three days rations, overcoats and rubber blankets. We guess that our men are going to guard some prisoners from here to somewhere else. As I just came off guard this morning it is not my turn to be on duty next, so I do not go on this excursion and I am glad of it, for the nights are cold and it might rain.

Alex Douglas is still here, but expects to have a furlough soon. He has a 20 days sick furlough, but a good many here say he will never soldier in this regt. again. Think he will get his discharge.

I don't know as I want anything except some woolen socks. Uncle Sam charges .35 for socks. I have had only one pair from him and they are not like home made socks. Two prs. will be a great plenty for me. I think that we will stay here this winter. A good many of the men think so. We have two stoves in our quarters and things are being fixed up comfortably.

A young fellow's wife came the other night. He belongs to our Co. On being wakened up in the night he said to his wife when he saw her: "What in hell did you come for!" The Lieut. got up and gave her his bed. She is going to cook for the two Lieuts.

James gave me a letter. I suppose that when he is not studying he does not feel like writing. I know I should feel so if I were in his place. You misunderstand me about demerits at West Point. James said in his letter 100 demerits in six months after the second half year, but 150 the first and second half years. Does Alex have any good reading? Then I was down to see him he had a .25 novel to read. Not very useful reading.

I have learned to play checkers. Am quite interested in the game. But I shall not learn to play cards. It is a waste of time if nothing worse.

I hope Mrs. Brikerhoff will live with you this winter. It will be a great deal more pleasant for you. I am afraid Frances will have a hard time this winter in getting to school. Have you got any fodder so that you can keep pony? I think Frances ought to have a resting spell. She teaches too constantly. She is a dear, conscientious girl. She ought to enjoy life as she goes along. Hoping that you both will take the world easy I will close. Please write often.

From your aff. son,

C. F. Hubbell

P.S. I leave in the morning on another detail. This makes two squads that leave tomorrow. I take two days rations.

author: charles
sigSummary: The brothers meet by chance at a Washington depot — Charles falls out of dress parade to find Alex, only to watch the train pull a mile down the track to keep soldiers out of the city. Bound for Tennessee with the 11th and 12th Corps to reinforce Rosecrans, Alex is healthy, sunburnt, a moustache sprouting, weary of Virginia: "while they were riding they were not fighting." Charles had just guarded 282 ragged rebel prisoners down the Potomac to Point Lookout.
transcription:
September 29, 1863
Capitol Hill
Washington, D.C.

Dear Mother:

I wrote you a few days since, but will write you again to let you know I have seen Alex. He requested me to inform you about him. Last night while our Co. were drawn up to go out on dress parade who should I see but Alex. He told me that he had only a few moments to stay, so the orderly sergt. said I could fall out. But as I could not get a man to leave camp till after parade he staid in our barracks a short time and then I went with him to the depot, but we found the train had left. We were both annoyed but went to an office close by to get transportation. Alex was told to wait and jam on the next train which would be along in about an hour. Alex said this was the first chance he had got into, but his Capt. would make it all right. His Capt. gave him his permission to leave. Well, after waiting some time, who should come along but two fellows of Alex's Co. They said the train was about one mile down the track where it had stopped and they took the chance to leave and go into the city. The train left the depot to prevent the soldiers from going into the city. Well, we reached the train and I staid there some time before the train started. Alex was glad to get the take to his co. He looked healthy, but is much sunburnt. Has a moustache sprouting out. I saw Amos Luther. He was well and had not a vine in his mouth. He is now sergt. The train was very long, a freight car with benches in them. A sentry was placed before the door of nearly all the cars, but they were not strict, and a good many of the men went into the city. I bet several going back to the arts. Alex is on his way to Tennessee. The 11th and 12th corps and I don't know but another one are going to reinforce Rosecrans. I asked Alex how he liked going off there. He said that he did not care where they went, that while they were riding they were not fighting, and he had gotten sick of Va.; it was nothing but a waste. He was glad I was in so good quarters.

I left Saturday A.M. with 75 of our regt. and we took 282 rebel prisoners from the old Capitol prison down to Point Lookout Out which is near the mouth of Chesapeake Bay. This Point L. is not far from Fortress Monroe. There are about 3000 prisoners confined there. We went on a steamer and had a fine ride down the Potomac and Bay. Arrived here Sunday night. All the N.C. Officers not on duty went on this trip as there were not men enough. Corporals were as thick as blackberries. The other squad of men started a little earlier in the morning than we did on a foot 350 deserters to Gen'l. Meade's Headquarters. They came back a little before me and I was told by some of them that the 11th and 12th corps were preparing to go to Tennessee.

The rebels were poorly dressed and had no uniforms, dressing as they pleased. Some of them were quite ragged, others had on near gray jackets drawn from their quartermasters. One of them said they were allowed $160 a year for clothing, but I don't think this is much as their currency has depreciated so much. They don't think much of their money as they gave a man for our Co. a $10 bill. One of them said green-backs were good anywhere they went. Said they rec'd $24 a month wages. I heard them talking about a good many taking the oath of allegiance. They did not like it, but they said their army was all the better for getting rid of bad men. A good many of the rebs have taken the oath and are then sent to Philadelphia not to come south of that during the war.

Lieut. Knapp of our Co. has gone home to Moorestown on leave of absence. Alex D. has not gotten his furlough yet. I heard not long since that Capt. Rich brought 1100 conscripts from N.Y. to Alex. Our Co. had just come off drill one day and were in line when Capt. Rich came and saw the Co. He did not have much to say to it. He then went back to N.Y. All the men like Capt. Rich.

Have you heard from James and Alex lately? James has owed me a letter for some time, but I suppose he is very busy in the reason. My health is good and I hope that I will stand the winter. But we may not have much of one, but may ride. How is your health and Frances and how does the world go with you both? Hope that you have wood enough to keep warm this cold weather. The weather is warm and pleasant here now. The cold rains are to come.

From your aff. son

C. F. Hubbell
